summary: Describes the vacation extension to Sieve, an autoresponder like the Unix vacation command. It includes safety features to avoid problems such as message loops. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5230 adds a vacation auto-reply action to Sieve, an email filtering language. It limits repeat replies and blocks many messages that should not receive an automatic response, helping prevent mail loops and unwanted notices.

questions: what is the sieve vacation extension
how does sieve vacation avoid mail loops
what does the vacation days parameter do
subtitle: Adds a controlled vacation auto-reply action to the Sieve email filtering language.

tldr.problem: People need to tell senders that they may not read or answer email promptly, without creating reply loops or sending repeated notices.
tldr.mechanism: The Sieve vacation action sends a reply to the original envelope sender and tracks previous responses, with limits on who receives a reply and how often.
tldr.outcome: Sieve scripts can generate personalized absence notices while avoiding common automated-mail hazards. RFC 5230 is updated by RFC 8580.

facts.label: Default response tracking period
facts.value: 7 days or the site's minimum, whichever is greater

today: RFC 5230 is a Proposed Standard for the Sieve vacation extension and is updated by RFC 8580.

sections.title: The Vacation Action
sections.content:
The vacation extension lets a Sieve script send a message explaining that a recipient will not answer promptly. The extension is identified by the capability name vacation.

The action sends its response to the Return-Path address, which represents the envelope sender of the message being handled. A script can choose the response text and optional parameters such as a subject, sender address, and message format.
sections.plainLanguage: A Sieve vacation action automatically tells an email sender that a reply may be delayed. The response goes to the original message's envelope sender.

sections.title: When Replies Are Repeated
sections.content:
The :days parameter controls how long the system remembers a response to an address. If omitted, the default is seven days or the site's minimum, whichever is greater.

Tracking considers both the recipient and the response content, unless the script supplies a shared :handle. This means different kinds of vacation notices can be sent separately, while identical notices are not repeated too often.
sections.plainLanguage: The server remembers whom it has already answered and which notice it sent. This prevents repeated identical replies during the configured period while allowing a different notice when the script calls for one.

sections.title: Who Should Receive an Auto-Reply
sections.content:
The action must not reply unless one of the recipient's own addresses appears in a direct recipient field such as To, Cc, or Bcc. The implementation can identify the user's address from its own records, the final envelope recipient, or the script's :addresses list.

Implementations must maintain a list of addresses that never receive vacation messages, and should avoid replying to messages marked as automated or as mailing-list traffic. A script can use the action only once, and it cannot be combined with Sieve reject or refuse actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The action replies only to messages addressed directly to the user, not messages copied through a list or sent to an unrelated recipient. Servers also block replies to addresses and messages that appear automated.

sections.title: Building the Response Message
sections.content:
The response body comes from the action's reason string. Without a custom subject, the response subject begins with Auto: and the original subject; if the original has no subject, the implementation should use a fixed default.

Responses should identify themselves with an Auto-Submitted header and include the original Message-ID in In-Reply-To. The optional :mime parameter treats the reason as a MIME entity; otherwise it is UTF-8 text.
sections.plainLanguage: The script supplies the message text, and the server builds the reply headers. Those headers mark the message as automatic and connect it to the original email when a Message-ID is available.

sections.title: Safety and Security
sections.content:
Implementations must not send responses to messages that were not sent directly to the user, and must honor the configured response interval. These rules reduce the chance of loops and repeated mail.

The RFC refers to the broader security guidance for automatic email responses. It says the extension adds no additional security concerns in that general area, but faulty implementation of its restrictions can cause unwanted messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The main safeguards are to reply only to direct personal messages and not more often than allowed. These rules help keep auto-replies from creating loops or flooding other systems.
